title: REST API Design
summary: Resources, verbs, and status codes as the core REST mental model — the vocabulary every other API-design topic assumes you already have.

slides.markdown:
REST models an API as a set of **resources** (nouns) that you act on with a small, fixed set of HTTP verbs — instead of a pile of one-off action endpoints. `/users/42` plus `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE` replaces `/getUser`, `/updateUser`, `/deleteUser`.

Think of it like a filing cabinet: the resource is the folder, and the verb is what you do to it (read it, replace it, remove it) — the folder's name never changes based on the action. This topic is the base vocabulary every other API-design topic builds on.

slides.sectionTitle: Resources, not actions: the REST mental model
slides.markdown:
A **resource** is a noun your system cares about — a user, an order, an invoice — addressed by a URL: `/orders/1024`. The HTTP verb, not the URL, carries the action. This is the single biggest shift from RPC-style thinking, where every operation gets its own named endpoint (`/createOrder`, `/cancelOrder`).

Modeling resources first forces a useful discipline: you have to name the *thing*, not the *operation*, which tends to produce a smaller, more predictable surface. A `Order` resource naturally supports create/read/update/cancel through the same URL and different verbs, instead of four unrelated endpoint names to memorize.

The takeaway: before writing a route, ask "what noun is this?" — the verbs almost always follow.

slides.sectionTitle: HTTP verbs mapped to CRUD, and where that mapping breaks down
slides.markdown:
The standard mapping: `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT` replaces the whole resource, `PATCH` partially updates it, `DELETE` removes it. `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are meant to be **idempotent** — calling them twice has the same effect as once — while `POST` is not.

The mapping breaks down for actions that aren't CRUD at all: approving an expense report, sending a password-reset email, or merging two records don't map cleanly to "replace" or "delete." Forcing them into `PUT`/`DELETE` produces awkward, unintuitive APIs.

The common fix is a **sub-resource verb-as-noun**: model the action itself as a resource you create, e.g. `POST /orders/1024/cancellations` instead of a raw `POST /orders/1024/cancel`. It keeps the noun-first discipline even for one-off actions.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a resource hierarchy as URLs
slides.markdown:
![Nested resource hierarchy from customers collection down to a single order item](assets/resource-hierarchy.svg)

URLs read as a path through nested resources: `/customers` is a **collection**, `/customers/42` is a single **item** inside it, and `/customers/42/orders` is that customer's own collection of orders. The pattern repeats: collection, item, nested collection.

The practical rule: a collection URL never has a trailing action baked in (`/customers/active` is fine as a filtered view, `/customers/getActive` is not) — filtering belongs in query params, not the path.

slides.sectionTitle: Status codes that actually communicate the right thing
slides.markdown:
Status codes are a contract, not decoration: a client's retry logic, alerting, and error handling all branch on them. `200 OK` for a successful `GET`/`PUT`/`PATCH`, `201 Created` for a successful `POST` that made something new (with a `Location` header pointing at it), `204 No Content` for a successful `DELETE` with nothing to return.

On failure, the split that matters most: `4xx` means the client's request was wrong (`400` malformed, `401` unauthenticated, `403` unauthorized, `404` not found, `409` conflict) and retrying the same request won't help; `5xx` means the server failed and a retry might succeed.

A common mistake is returning `200 OK` with an error message in the body — it silently defeats every piece of tooling (monitoring, caching, client retry logic) that reads the status line instead of parsing the payload.

| | REST (resource-oriented) | RPC-style (action-oriented) |
|---|---|---|
| URL shape | Nouns: `/orders/1024` | Verbs: `/getOrder`, `/cancelOrder` |
| Verb carries meaning | Yes — `GET`/`POST`/`DELETE` all differ | No — usually always `POST` |
| Caching | Falls out of `GET` + URL for free | Needs explicit cache-control design |
| Fits naturally | CRUD-shaped resources | One-off actions, batch operations, RPC-native systems (gRPC) |

**How to decide:** if the domain is genuinely resource-shaped (users, orders, documents), REST's conventions save you from reinventing status codes and caching. If most operations are commands with no natural "resource" (`processPayment`, `runReport`), an RPC style — or a hybrid, resources for nouns and a few verb-shaped endpoints for real actions — is often the honest choice.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a well-designed REST endpoint set for one resource
slides.markdown:
```
GET    /invoices              # list invoices (supports ?status=paid&limit=20)
POST   /invoices              # create an invoice -> 201 Created, Location: /invoices/9001
GET    /invoices/9001         # fetch one invoice -> 200 OK, or 404 if missing
PATCH  /invoices/9001         # partially update (e.g. { "status": "paid" }) -> 200 OK
DELETE /invoices/9001         # remove -> 204 No Content
POST   /invoices/9001/void    # one-off action modeled as a sub-resource -> 201 Created
```

Notice the pattern holds even for the non-CRUD action: `void` isn't a query param or a verb bolted onto the URL, it's its own nested resource creation.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: verbs in the URL and inconsistent status codes
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "It doesn't matter if the URL says `/getUser/42` as long as it returns the right data."

**Why it's wrong:** a verb baked into the URL (`/getUser`, `/updateUser`) duplicates what the HTTP method already says, and it tends to spread — soon there's `/getUserOrders`, `/deleteUserOrder`, each with its own inconsistent status-code habits (one team's `/deleteUser` returns `200` with a body, another's returns `204`). Clients end up writing bespoke handling per endpoint instead of trusting a shared convention.

**Correct model:** the noun lives in the URL, the verb lives in the HTTP method, and status codes follow the same convention everywhere in the API — so a client can write one generic "handle 2xx / 4xx / 5xx" path instead of one per endpoint.

slides.subTitle: Versioning
slides.markdown:
Resources and status codes solve today's contract, but every REST API eventually needs a way to change that contract without breaking clients already depending on it. Three approaches, in order of how commonly they're used in practice: **URI versioning** (`/v1/orders`, `/v2/orders`) is the most explicit and the easiest for clients to reason about, at the cost of maintaining parallel routes. **Header/content-negotiation versioning** (`Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json`) keeps URLs clean but is easy for clients to misconfigure, since the version lives somewhere less visible. **Field-additive, no version number** treats every change as backward-compatible by only ever adding optional fields, never removing or repurposing one — this avoids versioning entirely but requires strict discipline from every future contributor.

Concrete example: Stripe's API uses a dated version string per account (`2024-06-20`) rather than a `v1`/`v2` scheme, letting each integration pin to the contract it was built against indefinitely while new accounts default to the latest.

The takeaway: URI versioning is the most common default for public REST APIs specifically because it's the most discoverable — a client can see which contract they're on just by reading the URL.
